The cathedral's at the top of the avenue. If he's anywhere, he's up there.
Head up the avenue to the cathedral steps.
Evernoon is Aurenne, forty years ago, on the afternoon of a festival. The people here are Remembrances. They sway like a held note.
The dancers stand aside, smiling, very still.
Five dancers, linked by ribbons, mid-step across the foot of the cathedral steps. Their skirts are lifted in a turn that never finishes.
Pardon us. Excuse — pardon — they will not budge. Not rudely. They just... don't.
Could go round.
There is no round. The steps are the only way up. I checked. Twice.
Could go _over_.
Pip tries. He bounces off a ribbon as if it were an iron bar.
They are waiting for the next beat of the music. The music is waiting for the next minute. The minute is waiting.
For what?
For the clocks. In his memory, every square in Aurenne had a sundial. They all say noon.
Then we make them say something else.
Wake the three sundials — in the market (west), the gardens (east) and the bell-tower square (north-west).
A frozen procession blocks the cathedral. Sable says the minute is waiting for the clocks. We're going to make the sundials move.
The shadow has slipped one minute past noon. It feels like a door left open.
A sundial. Its shadow points straight up at noon. It looks as if it has never pointed anywhere else.
The shadow points at noon. Wren lifts her hand, and the Lanternkeeper's light gathers in her palm — the light her mother carried every night of her life.
Come on. One minute. Just give me one.
The shadow trembles... and slides, a hair's breadth, to one minute past noon.
Somewhere across the city, a clock remembers how to tick.
One. Single. Tick.
The dancers finish their turn. They curtsy to nobody. Then they drift aside, smiling, and go very still again — out of the way.
Well. That's the first thing that's happened here in forty years.
It felt good. Did you feel it? Like a breath let out.
The procession has parted. Climb the steps and enter the cathedral.
We woke all three sundials. Time moved one minute in Evernoon, and the procession let us pass.
A bench at the top of the steps. A plate with two honeycakes on it. One half-eaten. One untouched.
That one is hers. He is still saving it for her.
The First Watch
Squire Venn
First watch tonight. I'm— I'm going to do it scared.
Sir. Thank you, sir.
My token! "Come home safe." She scratched that with a hairpin. I'd have died of shame if I'd lost it.
Sir — you're a knight, aren't you? A real one. You've got the look.
Were you scared? Your first watch?
I'm scared now.
Oh. Good. I mean — not good. But good.
Here is what someone very wise once told me. You will be afraid. Do it anyway. That's the whole secret. There isn't a better one.
Do it anyway.
Here. Take this — it's my squire's badge. Tin. Not worth much. I've got a spare.
He hasn't got a spare. There is a clean, pale square on his surcoat where it was pinned.
_(very quietly)_ He always did that. Gave you the thing and said he had another.
Bram met Sir Aldous, seventeen and terrified of his first watch. Bram told him what Aldous once told him. He called himself a knight. He didn't even stumble over it.
It's a little tin sun. I had it by the fountain, I'm sure I did...
H-halt! Who goes— oh. Festival-goers. Sorry. Sorry! First posting.
Bram? Bram, you've gone white.
That's him. That's Sir Aldous. He's— he's younger than me. Look at him. He's a _child_.
Squire Aldous Venn, Dawnguard. First night watch tonight. On the Lantern plaza. Which is an honor. A large honor. I am large-ly honored.
Only I've lost my token. Mum gave it me. For luck. I had it by the fountain, and now...
We'll find it. I— we'll find it. Squire.
Young Squire Aldous Venn lost his mother's tin sun token near the festival fountain (south plaza). Find it for him.
Something glints in the fountain's basin, under water that has not rippled in forty years.
Come home safe. ...Right. Back to the post.
